# Introduction

In this section, we show how to merge, collapse and reshape the various data structures within a given sweep of Next Steps to create a dataset at the cohort member-level (i.e., one row per cohort member). This is likely to be the most useful data structure for most analyses.

[Most Next Steps files already have one row per cohort member](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/next_steps-data_structures.html) and all files are linked with a single identifier, `NSID`, so combining data within a sweep is more straightforward than in, e.g., the [MCS](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/mcs-merging_within_sweep.html). There are two complications. First, information about cohort members' parents is stored in separate variables for the "main parent" and "second parent", so some work is required to create variables that summarise both parents or that relate to a particular parent (such as the mother). Second, a small number of files - notably the household grid - have more than one row per cohort member and need to be collapsed before they are merged with other data.

We begin by clearing any data and programs from `Stata`'s memory (`clear all`) and telling `Stata` not to pause when displaying long output (`set more off`):

```{stata}
clear all
set more off
```

# Data Cleaning

We create a small dataset that contains information from Sweep 1 on: the cohort member's sex and attitude to school, housing tenure, family social class (National Statistics Socio-economic Classification; NS-SEC), mother's social class, and the number of siblings living with the cohort member. Constructing and combining these variables involves restructuring the data in various ways, and spans the most common data engineering tasks involved in bringing together information from a single sweep.

We use three datasets: the young person file (`safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_young_person_2020.dta`) and the family background file (`safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020.dta`), which both have one row per cohort member, and the household grid (`household_grids/wave_one_lsype_household_grid_file_2020.dta`), which has one row per household member. Note, the household grid is stored in a different subfolder to the young person and family background files.

We begin with the simplest variables: the cohort member's sex and their attitude to school. These are stored in a cohort-member level dataset already (`wave_one_lsype_young_person_2020`), so they do not need further processing. Below we load the relevant variables along with the cohort member identifier, `NSID`, rename them, and save the result as a new dataset (`df_yp.dta`).

```{stata}
use NSID W1sexYP W1yschat1 using "safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_young_person_2020.dta", clear
rename (W1sexYP W1yschat1) (sex school_attitude)
save "df_yp.dta", replace
```

Housing tenure is a characteristic of the household and is stored in the family background file (`wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020`). As there is one cohort member per family in Next Steps, this file also has one row per cohort member, and the variable does not need any further processing at this stage.

```{stata}
use NSID W1hous12HH using "safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020.dta", clear
rename W1hous12HH tenure
save "df_tenure.dta", replace
```

Next, we create a variable for family social class using data on both parents. The family background file contains the NS-SEC of the main parent (`W1nssecMP`) and the second parent (`W1nssecSP`). As these are stored in separate *columns* (rather than separate rows), we can create a summary variable by operating across the columns. We first replace values outside the range 1-8 with `.` (negative values denote various forms of missingness - for instance, `-98` indicates there is no second parent in the household). We then take the minimum of the two variables using `egen` with the `rowmin()` function (lower values of NS-SEC indicate higher social class). `rowmin()` returns the minimum for each row, ignoring missing values, so where NS-SEC is only available for one parent, that parent's value is used.[^1]

[^1]: `wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020` also contains a derived variable for family NS-SEC, `W1nssecfam`, which is instead based on the occupation of the household reference person. We create our own variable here to demonstrate the principle, which can be applied to any pair of `MP` and `SP` variables.

```{stata}
use NSID W1nssecMP W1nssecSP using "safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020.dta", clear
replace W1nssecMP = . if !inrange(W1nssecMP, 1, 8) // Values outside 1-8 denote various forms of missingness
replace W1nssecSP = . if !inrange(W1nssecSP, 1, 8)
egen family_nssec = rowmin(W1nssecMP W1nssecSP) // Lowest value of the two variables in each row
keep NSID family_nssec
save "df_nssec.dta", replace
```

We next show a different way of using the main and second parent variables: reshaping the data from wide to long so that we have one row per *parent*. This is useful where we want to create a variable for a particular parent - in this case, the cohort member's mother. [The main and second parent are roles in the interview](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/next_steps-data_structures.html), and either could be the cohort member's mother, so we need to bring in information from the household grid to find out who each parent is.

The family background file contains the variables `W1mainres` and `W1secores`, which record the person number of the main and second parent in the household grid. Below, we first rename these variables so that they follow the same convention as the NS-SEC variables (a common stub, followed by `MP` or `SP`). We then reshape the data from [wide to long using `reshape long`](https://www.stata.com/manuals/dreshape.pdf). We list the stubs (`W1HhID` and `W1nssec`) in the main command; these become the names of the variables in the reshaped dataset. The identifier is given in `i()`, and the suffixes (`MP` and `SP`) are stored in a new variable, `parent`, which is named in `j()`. The `string` option is needed as the suffixes are text rather than numbers. The result is a dataset with two rows per cohort member, one for each parent, which we save as `temp_parent.dta`.[^2]

[^2]: `reshape long` stacks the main and second parent variables on top of each other, and each of the reshaped variables keeps just one set of value labels. This does not matter here, as we only use the numeric values of these variables. For more on reshaping data, see [*Reshaping Data from Long to Wide (or Wide to Long)*](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/next_steps-reshape_long_wide.html).

```{stata}
use NSID W1mainres W1secores W1nssecMP W1nssecSP using "safeguarded_eul/wave_one_lsype_family_background_2020.dta", clear
rename (W1mainres W1secores) (W1HhIDMP W1HhIDSP)
reshape long W1HhID W1nssec, i(NSID) j(parent) string // One row per parent
save "temp_parent.dta", replace
```

The dataset now contains the person number of each parent (`W1HhID`). We can use this to merge in each parent's sex (`W1Sex`) and relationship to the cohort member (`W1R_1`) from the household grid (see [*Working with the Household Grid*](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/next_steps-household_grid.html)). Below, we load these variables from the household grid and use `joinby` to combine them with the parent-level dataset. `joinby NSID W1HhID` joins the rows of the two datasets that have the same `NSID` and `W1HhID`, and drops rows that do not have a match in the other dataset, so we only keep rows where the parent is found in the household grid (this drops, for instance, rows for second parents in families where there is no second parent). We use `joinby` rather than `merge 1:1` as it does not require `NSID` and `W1HhID` to uniquely identify the rows of each dataset, which may not be the case in the parent-level dataset (for instance, where the person numbers of both parents are recorded with the same missing value). We then keep the rows for natural mothers (`W1R_1 == 8` \[Natural parent\] and `W1Sex == 2` \[Female\]); `bysort NSID: gen n = _N` followed by `keep if n == 1` ensures there is only one natural mother identified per cohort member. The result is a dataset with one row per cohort member whose natural mother was the main or second parent, containing the mother's NS-SEC.[^3]

[^3]: More detail on merging datasets is provided in [*Combining Data Across Sweeps*](https://cls-data.github.io/data-handling-stata/docs/next_steps-merging_across_sweeps.html). Note, for many characteristics, the family background file already contains derived variables for mothers and fathers - in this case, `W1nssecmum` and `W1nssecdad`. The approach here is needed for `MP` and `SP` variables that do not have such an equivalent.

```{stata}
use NSID W1HhID W1Sex W1R_1 using "household_grids/wave_one_lsype_household_grid_file_2020.dta", clear
joinby NSID W1HhID using "temp_parent.dta" // Keeps matched rows only
keep if W1R_1 == 8 & W1Sex == 2
bysort NSID: gen n = _N
keep if n == 1
gen mother_nssec = W1nssec if inrange(W1nssec, 1, 8)
keep NSID mother_nssec
save "df_mother_nssec.dta", replace
```

Finally, we create a variable for the number of siblings living with the cohort member. This involves collapsing the household grid, which has one row per household member, so that it has one row per cohort member. `W1R_1` records each household member's relationship to the cohort member, with values between 13 and 17 indicating different types of sibling (natural, half-, step-, adopted and foster siblings). We first create a variable, `sibling`, which is equal to `1` where a household member is a sibling of the cohort member and `0` otherwise. We then sum this variable using `collapse` with the `by()` option to ensure this is calculated per cohort member (`by(NSID)`).

```{stata}
use NSID W1HhID W1R_1 using "household_grids/wave_one_lsype_household_grid_file_2020.dta", clear
gen sibling = inrange(W1R_1, 13, 17)
collapse (sum) n_siblings = sibling, by(NSID)
save "df_siblings.dta", replace
```

The same principles apply to the "hierarchical" files from Sweeps 8 and 9 - for instance, `ns8_2015_children.dta`, which has one row for each of the cohort member's children. Note, though, that cohort members only appear in these files if they have at least one record (e.g., at least one child), so some care is needed when merging the collapsed data with other files: cohort members who do not appear in the file should typically be assigned a count of zero, rather than a missing value.

# Merging the Datasets

Now we have cleaned each variable, we can merge them together. The cleaned datasets are all at the cohort member level. We begin with `df_yp.dta` as this has all the cohort members participating at Sweep 1 in it. We then use `merge` to merge in other data. As `NSID` uniquely identifies cohort members, we use `merge 1:1 NSID` in each case. The `nogenerate` option ensures that `Stata` does not create the `_merge` variable, and the `keep(master match)` option keeps only observations from the master (already open) dataset; note, doing this successively means we keep all rows in `df_yp.dta` (and no more are added). Finally, we list the first ten rows of the merged dataset. By default, `list` splits a row across several lines where it is too wide for `Stata`'s output, so we first use `set linesize 255` to increase the maximum width of the output; each row of the listing then fits on a single line.

```{stata}
use "df_yp.dta", clear
merge 1:1 NSID using "df_tenure.dta", keep(master match) nogenerate
merge 1:1 NSID using "df_nssec.dta", keep(master match) nogenerate
merge 1:1 NSID using "df_mother_nssec.dta", keep(master match) nogenerate
merge 1:1 NSID using "df_siblings.dta", keep(master match) nogenerate
set linesize 255 // Widens the output so that each row of the listing fits on one line
list in 1/10
```

`merge` prints a table for each of the four merges, showing the number of cohort members who were and were not matched to a row in the dataset being merged in. (In the output of `list`, long variable names are shortened using a `~` - for instance, `family_nssec` is displayed as `family~c`.) Note, `merge 1:1` stops with an error if `NSID` is duplicated in either dataset. This is a useful check that the datasets have the structure we expect.
